newsitem.title: SAUDI ARABIA: Pilgrims mark Moslem feast, mourn fire victims.
newsitem.headline: Pilgrims mark Moslem feast, mourn fire victims.

text.p: Two million Moslems celebrated the Eid al-Adha feast on Thursday at the end of a haj pilgrimage in which 343 people died when a ferocious fire swept their camp.
Huge crowds performed early Eid prayers at the Grand Mosque in Mecca, while others made their way back to Mena, 11 km (seven miles) away, site of the Tuesday blaze that also injured 1,290.
As officials struggled to identify the dead, labourers finished erecting new tents to house pilgrims left without shelter after the inferno consumed 70,000 tents.

Moslems in seamless white robes hurled stones at three pillars symbolising the devil, while helicopters circled overhead. The stoning was the final ritual of the haj, which reached its climax on Wednesday at Mount Arafat where the Prophet Mohammad gave his last sermon 14 centuries ago.

"Oh my god, it was horrible," said Egyptian pilgrim Ehab, as he made his way back to the Mena tent site. "People were running everywhere, but they could not get away because everywhere they went they saw fire."
A Nigerian pilgrim said: "This was from god."
The Eid sermon made no mention of the fire. Thousands of worshippers shuffled shoulder-to-shoulder around the cube-shaped Kaaba at the centre of the Grand Mosque, one of Islam's holiest shrines.
The imam, who accused Israel of trying to seize Arab holy land and kill innocent civilians, said unity was essential to overcome attempts to weaken Islamic states.
Some pilgrims shaved their heads with bare blades, while others slaughtered sheep for Eid al-Adha -- the Feast of Sacrifice marked by a billion Moslems worldwide.

This year 500,000 sheep and 15,000 camels and cattle were being slaughtered, Saudi media said, adding that the meat would be distributed among the poor in 27 countries. Saudi television showed Mecca abattoir workers slitting the throats of struggling sheep.

Pilgrims, carrying umbrellas to ward off the sun in the 38 Celsius (100 Fahrenheit) heat, had to step over empty plastic water bottles and soft-drink cans littering the roads. At the site of the fire, the ground was strewn with burnt-out buses, melted electric fans and blackened metal tent frames.
Telephone lines were jammed as pilgrims called home from Mecca's 5,000 pay phones with Eid wishes and to reassure anxious relatives.

The official media did not give the nationalities of the dead but diplomats said most were Indians, Pakistanis and Bangladeshis. The fire also engulfed Syrian, Lebanese, Egyptian, Sudanese, Yemeni and Moroccan sections.
Diplomats said they still had no final figures on the number of their dead, adding that many bodies were charred beyond recognition.

"Saudi authorities said they will release the bodies of victims to the embassy after Eid...maybe early next week," an Indian embassy official told Reuters. "We will not know the exact figure until Saudi authorities inform us."

The blaze was the latest tragedy to strike the pilgrimage to Mecca, which able-bodied Moslems are obliged to perform at least once if they can afford it. In 1990, 1,426 pilgrims were crushed in a stampede in a tunnel and in 1994, another 270 people died in a stampede.
Riyadh has given no cause for Tuesday's blaze apart from saying it was an accident but diplomats and witnesses said it was caused by gas cylinders .
Staring blankly ahead, Saudi pilgrim Ahmed Kadar, 35, said pilgrims should be banned from using gas: "The fire was terrible. How can this happen?"
